title: Washing Our Hands of the Reading Wars
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: The author welcomes the mainstream surge of interest in the science of reading but worries that it will become one more fad in a fifty-year line of over-promised cures, from Whole Language to Balanced Literacy. The proposed alternative is to treat structured literacy as a standard of care rather than a cure-all, a non-negotiable foundation of how children are taught to read. The handwashing analogy carries the argument: we keep washing hands even though it does not prevent every infection, and we should keep teaching structured literacy even though it will not fix poverty or every reading gap. Open questions remain about content, scope and sequence, and grouping, and those are the conversations the field should be having. The piece is short but makes a clear and quotable case against hype cycles in literacy reform.
points: Past literacy reforms (Whole Language, Reading First, Balanced Literacy) were each sold as cure-alls and then abandoned when they underdelivered, and the author fears the same fate for the science of reading.
Structured literacy should be framed as a standard of care, as non-negotiable as handwashing, and not judged by whether it delivers perfect results.
Reading instruction cannot erase poverty, systemic racism, or neglect of schools, so claiming it can sets the movement up to fail.
The productive work now is the unresolved questions: which content to prioritise, what phonics sequence is optimal, and how to balance whole-class and small-group time.
quotes: For the last fifty years, we’ve been promised various cure-alls for our country’s reading woes: Whole Language, Reading First, Balanced Literacy, and more. All of them over-promised and under-delivered. When they failed to live up to the hype, we ditched them and moved on to the next fad.
I’m worried that this current moment will become just another passing reading fad that promises the moon and doesn’t deliver. So how do we avoid the hype cycle this time and do it differently?

We need to start talking and thinking about structured literacy not as a cure-all, but as a standard of care. It is not just the initiative of the decade; it’s a non-negotiable that rests at the foundation of all literacy instruction. It’s just how we teach kids to read. It’s how we care for our students, especially our most vulnerable and marginalized.

We also need to be real: structured literacy isn’t going to get every kid reading at grade level. It isn’t going to eradicate poverty, systemic racism, and generational neglect of our public schools and our teachers. These are powerful forces that can’t be defeated by changing how we teach reading.

At the beginning of the pandemic, we were told that handwashing would protect us from Covid-19. That guidance turned out to be largely wrong, but we haven’t stopped washing our hands. Handwashing is just something we do after going to the bathroom or getting our hands dirty. Even though handwashing doesn’t stop all contamination in hospitals or restaurants, it’s still mandatory because it’s critical to protecting our health.

The answers to these questions will vary depending on the teacher, the students, and their needs, but these are the kinds of thorny conversations educators should be diving into right now, instead of being dragged into yet another hype cycle about the latest, hottest, educational trend.
That stuff is all a distraction. Let’s all agree that the science of reading is not a panacea, but we need it anyway—just like we need to wash our hands after we go to the bathroom.
